text.tspan: The following is a simple example of an adjunction between categories that is not also an equivalence of
categories. Why do these two functors not define an equivalence of categories?
One way to confirm this is with the concept of full and faithful functors; if either L or R was a fully faithful
functor it could yield an equivalence of categories. A clear counterexample is 𝓒(2,1) = ∅, which maps to
p₁₂ is an arbitrary name for the one
These two functors are adjoint because of the existence of the object isomorphisms α₁₂ and α₂₂ in Set.
Because there are only two objects in 𝓒 and one object in 𝓓, we can say there is a natural isomorphism of
the hom-sets 𝓒(-,R-) and 𝓓(L-,-) for any c ∈ 𝓒 and d ∈ 𝓓 by providing only α₁₂ and α₂₂ (given below).
The functors 𝓒(-,R-) and 𝓓(L-,-) given below are both from 𝓒ᵒᵖ × 𝓓 → Set, so for a natural transformation
between them to exist the naturality square must be satisified for every functor in the product category
𝓒ᵒᵖ × 𝓓. The morphisms in a product category are constructed as pairs of arrows¹; call these (f,g) where f is
in 𝓒 and g is in 𝓓 (following footnote 8 in the text). Notice f is in 𝓒, but will have the same name in 𝓒ᵒᵖ (as is
conventional in opposite categories) despite reversing the direction of morphisms. We typically have names

What is a hom-functor? A functor must map both objects and morphisms across categories, in a way that
preserves identities and composition. A hom-set suggests an obvious map to the category of sets: every
pair of objects A,B in the category should get mapped to the set HomC(A,B). Let's start with a simple category:
In the opposite category this morphism is still
called p₁₂, but ironically points from 2 to 1. So
f: c→c' = 2→1 in 𝓒ᵒᵖ and f: c'→c = 1→2 in 𝓒.
The product category with 4 objects and 12 non-identity morphisms, and the obvious map to the category
What if we wanted to map the original category to the category of sets? We'd have to fix one of the two
arguments to HomC. Fixing the first argument to 1, the first argument to 2, etc:
In words, Hom(A,-) is a functor to get all morphisms that leave A (i.e. have A as a source). For example, all
the morphisms that leave 1 are Hom(1,-) i.e. id₁ (going to 1) and a (going to 2). Similarly, Hom(-,B) is a
functor to get all morphisms that enter B (have B as a target).
There's an obvious formula we've filled in above to define how the functor acts on the morphism "a" when
we fix the first argument. In words, we define a function that post-composes the morphism to be mapped
(a) with its argument (e.g. id₁, b). In terms of paths, we extend all the paths in the set Hom(A,B) with
whatever's needed to go from B to B' (a) and therefore the set Hom(A,B'). Said another way, Hom(A,-) is a
functor to get all morphisms with an object A as a source, so to go from one set of objects that have A as a
source to another set that have A as a source we should only need to translate the target of all the first set
of morphisms. The resulting morphisms should still all have A as a source. The target will need to be
translated the same for all morphisms, based on the unfixed morphism argument to the functor.
For the morphism a, in yellow we highlight extending the path where we fix the first argument to 1 and 2.
The second (unfixed) argument is always a:
It's not as obvious how to create a formula to act on morphisms for the functor that fixes the second
argument. The objects represent those that in Hom(-,B) have B as a target, so our formula needs to keep
targets the same while updating sources.
For the morphism b, in green we highlight extending the path where we fix the second argument to 1 and 2.
The first (unfixed) argument is always b:
Define Hom(h,B) as a function that precomposes with its unfixed argument, effectively prepending to all the
paths in Hom(A',B) the morphism from A and A' to get the set Hom(A,B). Alternatively, prepending to all the
paths in Hom(A,B) the morphism from A' and A to get the set Hom(A,B):
This approach provides us with a formula, but the morphism that results is in the opposite direction of what we
need it to be to preserve composition. Said another way, we've defined Hom(h,B) as a contravariant functor.
Alternatively, one can define a covariant functor on the opposite category (that still precomposes):
Defining a bifunctor that is covariant in both arguments:
We've also highlighted a naturality square in green and yellow for the morphism pair (b,a). If you have already
applied the arguments (A,B) to HomC it should not be a surprise that it doesn't matter if you change the first
argument from A to A' or the second argument from B to B' first; you should still end up with HomC(A',B').
